title: Counsels of Wisdom (Babylonian moral advice)
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L II.3, Counsels of Wisdom (ed. Z. J. Földi), SB -) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: The Counsels of Wisdom, text: 157 of 159 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (13 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
The advice warns against evil companions, careless and slanderous speech, quarrels and marrying a prostitute, and urges kindness to the needy, daily worship of one's god, and honest service.

The Counsels of Wisdom is a collection of Babylonian moral advice in about 160 lines, addressed by a father, perhaps a royal official, to his son: on speech, companions, kindness, worship and conduct. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/2/3/SB/-) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed manuscript with the most signs preserved there. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives. Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 157 of the 159 lines of the eBL edition (99%), from 13 tablets in the British Museum: K.13770 (Nineveh), BM.41931, BM.51070, K.8282 (Nineveh), K.3364 (Nineveh), BM.41682, BM.33851, K.7897 (Nineveh), K.8231 (Nineveh), 1882,0522.555 (Nineveh), F.144, BM.33496, K.10652 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 2 of the 159 lines of the eBL edition have no witness here with an open photograph: A+1 (only on VAT.17157, CBS.6059); A+2 (only on CBS.6059). Lines that survive only on tablets whose photographs are not openly licensed (for example in the Iraq Museum, Berlin, Istanbul, Ankara, Philadelphia or private collections), or only on tablets whose eBL photograph does not show the lines, are omitted.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

translation.text:
27“Hold your tongue, watch what you say,
28“A gentleman’s pride should be the high esteem of your speech.
29“Insolence (and) abuse should be abhorrent to you,
30“Talk of nothing demeaning, no untrue report.
31“The gossipy person is despicable.
32“Do not stand around where there is a crowd,
33“Do not press forward where there is a dispute.
34“They will make you incur an inevitable consequence from the dispute,
35“For then you will be made their witness,
36“They will carry you off to bolster a case not your own.
37“When confronted with a dispute, avoid it, do not get involved.
38“If it is a dispute with you, then put out the flame.
39“A dispute is a wide-open ambush,
40“A barrier of brush that conceals one’s opponent,
41“It brings to mind what he forgot and accuses a man.
42“Do no evil to the man who disputes with you,
43“Requite with good the one who does evil to you.
44“Adhere to just treatment of your enemy,

translation.text:
A+5“Look to the class leader …, do not …
A+6“Revere and hon[or th]is […].
A+7“Take pity on the w[eak] (and) [he]lpless,
A+8“Do not […] the miserable, do not ho[ld] them in contempt.
A+9“Do not condescend haughtily to them.
A+10“One’s god will be angry with him for that,
A+11“It is displeasing to Shamash, he will requite him with evil.
A+12“Give food to eat, beverage to drink,
A+13“Aspire to what is right, provide for and honor.
A+14“One’s god will be happy with him for that,
A+15“It is pleasing to Shamash, he will requite him with favor.
A+16“Do good deeds, always be obliging.
A+17“Do not make a slave girl important in (your) house,
A+18“She must not rule your pathway [lik]e a wife.
A+19“Do not conduct yourself according to what a young girl says,
A+20“And you do not go dow[n to …] of your […],
A+21“You must not hear your people saying,
A+22“‘In (that) household it is the slave girl who rules and is a spendthrift.’

translation.text:
A+47“Spotless business, spotless doer’.
A+48“If they give you an administrative position for king or god,
A+49“And, they having assigned you your duties, you can give orders,
A+50“Do not neglect your predecessor [who is now above you?],
A+51“You should come in regularly every day,
A+52“And you should always have a present with you.
A+53“That way, you will advance successfully.
A+54“Do not treat badly someone who is in conflict with you,
A+55“Even if you have the power to promo[te] or demote,
A+56“That way, you will hold the post a long time,
A+57“Do not … [the presents that you give?, may] they revert to you.
A+58“Do not make [a decision?] of life (or death),
A+59“That is an abomination to […] ….

A+98“On the basis of what you have learned, read from [the tablet]:
